questions.text:
Despite his initial hesitation, Rehman’s _________ to contribute to the success of the project never wavered.

Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: The blank names something that "never wavered" despite early hesitation: a firm determination. "Resolve" means firm determination. "Ambivalence" (mixed feelings) contradicts "never wavered", "satisfaction" does not fit "to contribute", and "revolve" is a verb meaning to rotate. So the answer is resolve.

questions.text:
Bird : Nest :: Bee : _______

Select the correct option to complete the analogy.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: A nest is the home a bird builds and lives in. The home of a bee is a hive. A kennel houses a dog, a lair is a wild animal's den and a hammock is a hanging bed.

questions.text: If \(Pe^{x} = Qe^{-x}\) for all real values of \(x\), which one of the following statements is true?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Rewrite as \(Pe^{2x} = Q\) for every real \(x\). The left side changes with \(x\) unless \(P = 0\), and then \(Q = 0\) too. Check the others: \(P = Q = 1\) gives \(e^{x} = e^{-x}\), true only at \(x = 0\); \(P = 1, Q = -1\) gives \(e^{x} = -e^{-x}\), impossible since both sides have opposite signs; \(\frac{P}{Q} = 0\) needs \(P = 0\) with \(Q \neq 0\), which gives \(0 = Qe^{-x} \neq 0\). So \(P = Q = 0\).

questions.text:
The paper as shown in the figure is folded to make a cube where each square corresponds to a particular face of the cube. Which one of the following options correctly represents the cube?

Note: The figures shown are representative.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Take the square with the hollow triangle as the front. The square with the filled circle (above it in the net) folds to the top, the square with the hollow circle (below it) folds to the bottom, the two blank squares beside it fold to the left and right, and the square with the filled triangle (two squares to the right) folds to the back, opposite the hollow triangle.

(A) Front hollow triangle, top filled circle, right blank: consistent.
(B) Shows the filled triangle on a face adjacent to the hollow triangle, but they are opposite faces: impossible.
(C) With the hollow triangle upright, the top face must carry the filled circle, but it is blank: wrong.
(D) Shows the filled triangle on the top, adjacent to the hollow triangle: impossible.

So option (A).

questions.text: Let \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) denote two arbitrary prime numbers. Which one of the following statements is correct for all values of \(p_1\) and \(p_2\)?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p_1 + p_2\) is not a prime number.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p_1 p_2\) is not a prime number.

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: A product of two primes (each at least 2) has at least the divisors 1, \(p_1\), \(p_2\) and \(p_1p_2\), so it is never prime. Counterexamples for the rest: \(2 + 3 = 5\) is prime, so (A) fails; \(3 + 5 + 1 = 9\) is not prime, so (C) fails; \(3 \times 5 + 1 = 16\) is not prime, so (D) fails. Only (B) holds always.

questions.text:
Based only on the conversation below, identify the logically correct inference:

“Even if I had known that you were in the hospital, I would not have gone there to see you”, Ramya told Josephine.

options.label: A
options.text: Ramya knew that Josephine was in the hospital.

options.label: B
options.text: Ramya did not know that Josephine was in the hospital.

options.label: C
options.text: Ramya and Josephine were once close friends; but now, they are not.

options.label: D
options.text: Josephine was in the hospital due to an injury to her leg.

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: "Even if I had known" is a counterfactual: it describes a situation contrary to fact, so in reality Ramya did not know that Josephine was in the hospital. Nothing in the sentence speaks of their past friendship or the reason for the hospital stay, so (C) and (D) cannot be inferred, and (A) contradicts the counterfactual.

questions.text: If IMAGE and FIELD are coded as FHBNJ and EMFJG respectively then, which one among the given options is the most appropriate code for BEACH ?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Reverse the word, then shift each letter one place forward.
IMAGE reversed is EGAMI; each letter +1 gives FHBNJ.
FIELD reversed is DLEIF; each letter +1 gives EMFJG.
BEACH reversed is HCAEB; each letter +1 gives IDBFC.

questions.text:
Which one of the following options is correct for the given data in the table?

| Iteration (\(i\)) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Input (\(I\)) | 20 | \(-4\) | 10 | 15 |
| Output (\(X\)) | 20 | 16 | 26 | 41 |
| Output (\(Y\)) | 20 | \(-80\) | \(-800\) | \(-12000\) |
questions.subject: General Aptitude

questions.text:
In the given figure, PQRS is a square of side 2 cm and PLMN is a rectangle. The corner L of the rectangle is on the side QR. Side MN of the rectangle passes through the corner S of the square.

What is the area (in cm\(^2\)) of the rectangle PLMN?

Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Triangle PLS has base PL (a side of the rectangle) and its vertex S lies on the opposite side MN, so its height is PN. Hence area(PLS) \(= \frac{1}{2}\) area(PLMN).
Also, triangle PLS has base PS (a side of the square, 2 cm) and its vertex L lies on QR, the opposite side of the square, so its height is 2 cm. Area(PLS) \(= \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 2 = 2\) cm\(^2\).
So area(PLMN) \(= 2 \times 2 = 4\) cm\(^2\).

questions.text:
The diagram below shows a river system consisting of 7 segments, marked P, Q, R, S, T, U, and V. It splits the land into 5 zones, marked Z1, Z2, Z3, Z4, and Z5. We need to connect these zones using the least number of bridges. Out of the following options, which one is correct?

Note: The figure shown is representative.

options.label: A
options.text: Bridges on P, Q, and T

options.label: B
options.text: Bridges on P, Q, S, and T

options.label: C
options.text: Bridges on Q, R, T, and V

options.label: D
options.text: Bridges on P, Q, S, U, and V

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Read which two zones each segment separates: P (Z1, Z2), R (Z2, Z3), Q (Z1, Z3), S (Z1, Z5), T (Z3, Z5), V (Z3, Z4), U (Z4, Z5). Connecting 5 zones needs at least 4 bridges forming a spanning tree, so (A) with 3 bridges is too few and (D) with 5 is not the least.
(B) P, Q, S, T joins Z1, Z2, Z3, Z5 but nothing reaches Z4.
(C) Q, R, T, V joins Z1-Z3, Z2-Z3, Z5-Z3, Z4-Z3: all five zones are connected with 4 bridges.
So (C).

questions.text: If \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\), then which ONE of the following is \(A^{8}\) ?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics

questions.text: The value of \(x\) such that \(x > 1\), satisfying the equation \(\int_{1}^{x} t \ln t \, dt = \frac{1}{4}\) is
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: By parts, \(\int t \ln t \, dt = \frac{t^{2}}{2}\ln t - \frac{t^{2}}{4}\). From 1 to \(x\): \(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\ln x - \frac{x^{2}}{4} + \frac{1}{4}\). Setting this equal to \(\frac{1}{4}\) gives \(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\ln x = \frac{x^{2}}{4}\), so \(\ln x = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(x = \sqrt{e}\).

questions.text:
Consider a binary tree \(T\) in which every node has either zero or two children. Let \(n > 0\) be the number of nodes in \(T\).

Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in \(T\) that have exactly two children?
questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution: Let \(i\) be the number of nodes with two children and \(l\) the number of leaves. Counting edges: every node except the root has one parent edge, so \(n - 1 = 2i\). Hence \(i = \frac{n-1}{2}\).

questions.text:
Let \(L\), \(M\), and \(N\) be non-singular matrices of order 3 satisfying the equations \(L^{2} = L^{-1}\), \(M = L^{8}\) and \(N = L^{2}\).

Which ONE of the following is the value of the determinant of \((M - N)\)?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: \(L^{2} = L^{-1}\) gives \(L^{3} = I\). Then \(M = L^{8} = L^{6}L^{2} = L^{2} = N\), so \(M - N\) is the zero matrix and its determinant is 0.

questions.text:
Let \(P(x)\) be an arbitrary predicate over the domain of natural numbers.

Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
(A) is the principle of mathematical induction over the naturals, valid for every \(P\).
(B) Take \(P(x)\) true only for \(x = 0\): the downward rule holds vacuously for \(x > 0\) and \(P(0)\) holds, but \(\forall x\, P(x)\) is false.
(C) Take \(P(x)\) true exactly for \(x \leq 1000\): both premises hold, the conclusion fails at 1001.
(D) Take \(P(x)\) true exactly for \(x \geq 1000\): both premises hold, the conclusion fails at 0.
So only (A) is true for an arbitrary predicate.

questions.text:
Consider the following statements:

(i) Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address.

(ii) A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgement for a segment from R to S.

Which ONE of the following is CORRECT?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution:
(i) True: ARP resolves an IP address to the MAC (link-layer) address on the local network.
(ii) False: TCP is full duplex and uses piggybacking, so one segment can carry data from S to R and also acknowledge data from R to S through its ACK flag and acknowledgement number.

questions.text:
Consider the routing protocols given in List I and the names given in List II:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| (i) Distance vector routing | (a) Bellman-Ford |
| (ii) Link state routing | (b) Dijkstra |

For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution: Distance vector routing computes routes with the distributed Bellman-Ford equation, exchanging distance vectors with neighbours. Link state routing floods link state packets so each router knows the whole topology, then runs Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm. So (i) to (a) and (ii) to (b).

questions.text:
A machine receives an IPv4 datagram. The protocol field of the IPv4 header has the protocol number of a protocol X.

Which ONE of the following is NOT a possible candidate for X?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution: The protocol field names the protocol carried directly inside the IP datagram. ICMP (1), IGMP (2) and OSPF (89) are carried directly in IP and have protocol numbers. RIP is an application-level protocol that runs over UDP (port 520), so the protocol field would say UDP (17), never RIP.

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
a holds "@#Hello World!" in a[0..13] with the terminating null at a[14]. stringcopy(a, a + 2) copies characters from a[2] onwards to a[0] onwards while the source character is not null. It copies the 12 characters "Hello World!" into a[0..11], then stops at the null at a[14] without copying it.

a[12] and a[13] still hold 'd' and '!' from the original string, and a[14] is still the null. So printf prints "Hello World!d!".

questions.text:
Consider an unordered list of \(N\) distinct integers.

What is the minimum number of element comparisons required to find an integer in the list that is NOT the largest in the list?
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution: Pick any two elements and compare them once. Since the integers are distinct, the smaller of the two is less than another element of the list, so it cannot be the largest. One comparison suffices, and zero comparisons cannot guarantee it.

questions.text:
Consider the following statements about the use of backpatching in a compiler for intermediate code generation:

(I) Backpatching can be used to generate code for Boolean expression in one pass.

(II) Backpatching can be used to generate code for flow-of-control statements in one pass.

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution: Backpatching leaves jump targets blank in lists (truelist, falselist, nextlist) and fills them in once the target address is known. This is exactly what lets both Boolean expressions with short-circuit jumps and flow-of-control statements (if, while) be translated in a single pass. Both statements are correct.

questions.text:
Given the following syntax directed translation rules:

Rule 1: \(R \rightarrow AB\) \(\{B.i = R.i - 1;\ A.i = B.i;\ R.i = A.i + 1;\}\)

Rule 2: \(P \rightarrow CD\) \(\{P.i = C.i + D.i;\ D.i = C.i + 2;\}\)

Rule 3: \(Q \rightarrow EF\) \(\{Q.i = E.i + F.i;\}\)

Which ONE is the CORRECT option among the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Rule 1 is S-attributed and L-attributed; Rule 2 is S-attributed and not L-attributed; Rule 3 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed

options.label: B
options.text: Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed; Rule 2 is S-attributed and L-attributed; Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed

options.label: C
options.text: Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed; Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed; Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed

options.label: D
options.text: Rule 1 is S-attributed and not L-attributed; Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed; Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
S-attributed means only synthesized attributes (head computed from body). L-attributed allows inherited attributes of a body symbol only from the head's inherited attributes and symbols to its LEFT.
Rule 1: \(A.i = B.i\) gives A an attribute from B, its right sibling, so it is not L-attributed, and since it has inherited attributes it is not S-attributed either.
Rule 2: \(D.i = C.i + 2\) is inherited from the left sibling C, which L-attribution allows, but the inherited attribute means it is not S-attributed.
Rule 3: \(Q.i = E.i + F.i\) is purely synthesized, so it is S-attributed and therefore also L-attributed.
This is option (C).

questions.text:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes.

Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution:
The IP payload is the whole UDP segment: \(7488 + 8 = 7496\) bytes (8 bytes of UDP header).
Each fragment can carry \(1500 - 20 = 1480\) bytes of IP payload, which is a multiple of 8, so all non-last fragments carry 1480 bytes.
\(7496 = 5 \times 1480 + 96\), so there are 5 full fragments and a 6th carrying 96 bytes.
The last fragment is \(96 + 20 = 116\) bytes including its header.

questions.text: Which ONE of the following languages is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton?

options.label: C
options.text: Any language accepted by a non-deterministic pushdown automaton.

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution: A DFA is a DPDA that never uses its stack, so every regular language is accepted by a DPDA. Not every context-free language is deterministic (for example, even-length palindromes \(ww^{R}\) need nondeterminism), and NPDAs accept exactly the CFLs, so (B) and (C) fail. Decidable languages include non-context-free ones such as \(a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}\), so (D) fails.

questions.text:
Let \(G_1, G_2\) be Context Free Grammars (CFGs) and \(R\) be a regular expression. For a grammar \(G\), let \(L(G)\) denote the language generated by \(G\).

Which ONE among the following questions is decidable?
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution: Emptiness of a CFG is decidable: mark the generating variables and check whether the start symbol is among them. Equivalence of two CFGs, emptiness of the intersection of two CFLs, and equality of a CFL with a regular language (which includes the undecidable question \(L(G_1) = \Sigma^{*}\)) are all undecidable.

questions.text:
Processes P1, P2, P3, P4 arrive in that order at times 0, 1, 2, and 8 milliseconds respectively, and have execution times of 10, 13, 6, and 9 milliseconds respectively. Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) algorithm is used as the CPU scheduling policy. Ignore context switching times.

Which ONE of the following correctly gives the average turnaround time of the four processes in milliseconds?
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
0 to 2: P1 runs (remaining 8). At 1, P2 (13) arrives and does not preempt.
At 2, P3 (6) arrives; 6 < 8, so P3 runs 2 to 8 and finishes. Turnaround \(8 - 2 = 6\).
At 8, P4 (9) arrives; remaining times P1 8, P2 13, P4 9. P1 runs 8 to 16. Turnaround 16.
P4 runs 16 to 25. Turnaround \(25 - 8 = 17\).
P2 runs 25 to 38. Turnaround \(38 - 1 = 37\).
Average \(= \frac{6 + 16 + 17 + 37}{4} = \frac{76}{4} = 19\) ms.

questions.text:
An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account \(A\) attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. 10000 each from account \(A\) to account \(B\). Both transactions read the same value, Rs. 11000, as the initial balance in \(A\) and were allowed to go through. \(B\) was credited Rs. 10000 twice. \(A\) was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. 1000.

Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
Both transfers read the balance Rs. 11000 before either wrote it, and each wrote Rs. 1000 back, so one debit was lost.

Isolation is violated: run one after the other, the second transfer would have read Rs. 1000, so this result can only come from the two interleaving.

Consistency is violated: B received Rs. 20000 while A lost only Rs. 10000, so the total money in the bank went up by Rs. 10000. A correct transfer never changes that total.

Atomicity is not shown to be violated: each transfer ran all of its steps. Durability is not either: no committed change was lost to a failure.

So B and C.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are part of an Instruction Set Architecture of a processor?

options.label: A
options.text: The size of the cache memory

options.label: B
options.text: The clock frequency of the processor

options.label: C
options.text: The number of cache memory levels

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
The ISA is the programmer-visible contract: instructions, addressing modes, data types and the architectural registers that instructions can name. The number of registers is part of it, since instructions encode register numbers.
Cache size, number of cache levels and clock frequency are implementation (microarchitecture) choices: different processors with the same ISA differ in them, and software does not have to change. So only (D).

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph G is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: A DFS tree of \(G\) is a Shortest Path tree of \(G\).

options.label: B
options.text: Every non-tree edge of G with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.

options.label: C
options.text: If \((u, v)\) is a non-tree edge of G with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from the source vertex \(s\) to \(u\) and \(v\) in the BFS tree are within \(\pm 1\) of each other.

options.label: D
options.text: Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of G.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution:
(A) False. In a triangle a, b, c with DFS from a going a to b to c, c is at depth 2 in the DFS tree though it is adjacent to a.
(B) True. In an undirected DFS there are no cross edges: every non-tree edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors, so it is a back edge (seen from the ancestor's side, a forward edge).
(C) True. BFS levels are the true distances, and for any edge \((u, v)\), \(d(v) \leq d(u) + 1\) and \(d(u) \leq d(v) + 1\), so the levels differ by at most 1.
(D) True. Restarting either traversal from an unvisited vertex finds one connected component per restart.

questions.text:
Consider the two lists List I and List II given below:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| (i) Context free languages | (a) Closed under union |
| (ii) Recursive languages | (b) Not closed under complementation |
| (iii) Regular languages | (c) Closed under intersection |

For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
Facts: CFLs are closed under union, not closed under complementation, not closed under intersection. Recursive languages are closed under union, complementation and intersection. Regular languages are closed under union, complementation and intersection.
An option is correct when every pairing in it is a true statement.
(A) (ii) to (b) says recursive languages are not closed under complementation: false.
(B) (i) to (b) true, (ii) to (a) true, (iii) to (c) true: correct.
(C) (i) to (b) true, (ii) to (c) true, (iii) to (a) true: correct.
(D) (iii) to (b) says regular languages are not closed under complementation: false.

questions.text:
Consider the following logic circuit diagram.

Which is/are the CORRECT option(s) for the output function \(F\)?
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
The OR gate's inputs are the NAND of X and Y, NOT X, and X AND NOT Y. So \(F = \overline{XY} + \overline{X} + X\overline{Y} = \overline{X} + \overline{Y} + \overline{X} + X\overline{Y} = \overline{X} + \overline{Y}\) (since \(X\overline{Y}\) is absorbed by \(\overline{Y}\)).
(A) \(\overline{XY} = \overline{X} + \overline{Y}\): correct.
(B) \(\overline{X} + \overline{Y} + X\overline{Y} = \overline{X} + \overline{Y}\): correct.
(C) is exactly the circuit's expression: correct.
(D) \(X + \overline{Y}\) at \(X = 0, Y = 1\) gives 0, but \(F = 1\): wrong.

questions.text:
The following two signed 2’s complement numbers (multiplicand M and multiplier Q) are being multiplied using Booth’s algorithm:

M: 1100 1101 1110 1101 and Q: 1010 0100 1010 1010

The total number of addition and subtraction operations to be performed is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
Booth's algorithm scans the multiplier pairs \((Q_i, Q_{i-1})\) with \(Q_{-1} = 0\): a pair 10 means subtract M, 01 means add M, 00 and 11 mean only shift. So the count of operations is the number of adjacent bit changes in Q with a 0 appended on the right.
Q with the extra 0: 1010 0100 1010 1010 0.
Reading 10100100101010100 left to right, the adjacent pairs are 10, 01, 10, 00, 01, 10, 00, 01, 10, 01, 10, 01, 10, 01, 10, 00. Every pair except the three 00 pairs is an operation.
That is \(16 - 3 = 13\) operations. So 13 additions and subtractions.

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
The loop is the subtraction form of Euclid's algorithm, so it ends with \(x = y = \gcd(126, 105)\).
Trace: (126, 105) to (21, 105) to (21, 84) to (21, 63) to (21, 42) to (21, 21). The loop stops and prints 21.

questions.text: In a 4-bit ripple counter, if the period of the waveform at the last flip-flop is 64 microseconds, then the frequency of the ripple counter in kHz is ________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution: Each flip-flop of a ripple counter divides the frequency by 2, so the last of 4 flip-flops runs at \(\frac{f_{clk}}{16}\). Its period is 64 \(\mu\)s, so its frequency is \(\frac{1}{64 \times 10^{-6}} = 15.625\) kHz. The clock (counter) frequency is \(16 \times 15.625 = 250\) kHz.

questions.text:
Suppose the values 10, \(-4\), 15, 30, 20, 5, 60, 19 are inserted in that order into an initially empty binary search tree. Let \(T\) be the resulting binary search tree.

The number of edges in the path from the node containing 19 to the root node of \(T\) is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution:
10 is the root. \(-4\) goes left of 10, 15 right of 10, 30 right of 15, 20 left of 30, 5 right of \(-4\), 60 right of 30, and 19 left of 20.
Path from 19 to the root: 19, 20, 30, 15, 10, which is 4 edges.

questions.text:
Suppose we are transmitting frames between two nodes using Stop-and-Wait protocol. The frame size is 3000 bits. The transmission rate of the channel is 2000 bps (bits/second) and the propagation delay between the two nodes is 100 milliseconds. Assume that the processing times at the source and destination are negligible. Also, assume that the size of the acknowledgement packet is negligible.

Which ONE of the following most accurately gives the channel utilization for the above scenario in percentage?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution:
Transmission time \(T_t = \frac{3000}{2000} = 1.5\) s. Propagation delay \(T_p = 0.1\) s.
Utilization \(= \frac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p} = \frac{1.5}{1.7} = 0.8823\), that is 88.23%.

questions.text:
Let \(G\) be an edge-weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights. Suppose a positive constant \(\alpha\) is added to the weight of every edge.

Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE about the minimum spanning trees (MSTs) and shortest paths (SPs) in \(G\) before and after the edge weight update?

options.label: A
options.text: Every MST remains an MST, and every SP remains an SP.

options.label: B
options.text: MSTs need not remain MSTs, and every SP remains an SP.

options.label: C
options.text: Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.

options.label: D
options.text: MSTs need not remain MSTs, and SPs need not remain SPs.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution:
Every spanning tree of an \(n\)-vertex graph has \(n - 1\) edges, so each tree's weight rises by exactly \((n - 1)\alpha\); the order of trees by weight is unchanged and every MST stays an MST.
A path's weight rises by \(\alpha\) times its number of edges, so paths with more edges are penalised more. Example: edges s to t of weight 3, and s to a, a to t of weight 1 each. The shortest path is s, a, t (weight 2). After adding \(\alpha = 2\), it costs 6 while the direct edge costs 5. So SPs need not remain SPs.

questions.text:
A meld operation on two instances of a data structure combines them into one single instance of the same data structure. Consider the following data structures:

P: Unsorted doubly linked list with pointers to the head node and tail node of the list.

Q: Min-heap implemented using an array.

R: Binary Search Tree.

Which ONE of the following options gives the worst-case time complexities for meld operation on instances of size \(n\) of these data structures?
questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution:
P: link the tail of the first list to the head of the second and update the tail pointer: \(\Theta(1)\).
Q: copy both arrays into one array of size \(2n\) and run bottom-up build-heap, which is linear: \(\Theta(n)\). Any meld must at least move the \(n\) elements of one array, so \(\Theta(n)\) is tight.
R: do an inorder traversal of each BST to get two sorted lists (\(\Theta(n)\)), merge them (\(\Theta(n)\)), and build a BST from the sorted list (\(\Theta(n)\)): \(\Theta(n)\) overall, and every node must be placed so it cannot be less.
So P: \(\Theta(1)\), Q: \(\Theta(n)\), R: \(\Theta(n)\).

questions.text:
For a direct-mapped cache, 4 bits are used for the tag field and 12 bits are used to index into a cache block. The size of each cache block is one byte. Assume that there is no other information stored for each cache block.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT option for the sizes of the main memory and the cache memory in this system (byte addressable), respectively?
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
A one-byte block needs 0 offset bits, so the address is tag + index \(= 4 + 12 = 16\) bits. Main memory \(= 2^{16}\) bytes \(= 64\) KB.
The cache has \(2^{12}\) lines of 1 byte each \(= 4\) KB.

questions.text:
Given a Context-Free Grammar \(G\) as follows:

\(S \rightarrow Aa \mid bAc \mid dc \mid bda\)

\(A \rightarrow d\)

Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
\(\text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{a, c\}\).
From the start state, on \(d\) we reach the state \(\{S \rightarrow d\cdot c,\ A \rightarrow d\cdot\}\). SLR reduces \(A \rightarrow d\) on every symbol of FOLLOW(A), including \(c\), while \(S \rightarrow d\cdot c\) shifts \(c\): a shift-reduce conflict. So G is not SLR(1).
In LR(1) items this state is \(\{[S \rightarrow d\cdot c, \$],\ [A \rightarrow d\cdot, a]\}\): reduce only on \(a\), shift on \(c\), no conflict.
After \(b\) then \(d\) we reach \(\{[S \rightarrow bd\cdot a, \$],\ [A \rightarrow d\cdot, c]\}\): shift on \(a\), reduce only on \(c\), no conflict.
These two states have different cores, so LALR merging does not combine them and introduces no conflict. Hence G is LALR(1) (and CLR(1)) but not SLR(1).

questions.text:
An array \(A\) of length \(n\) with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index \(1 \leq i \leq n\) such that \(A[1..i]\) is sorted in the non-decreasing order and \(A[i+1..n]\) is sorted in the non-increasing order.

Which ONE of the following represents the best possible asymptotic bound for the worst-case number of comparisons by an algorithm that searches for an element in a bitonic array \(A\)?
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution:
Find the peak by binary search: compare \(A[mid]\) with \(A[mid + 1]\); if \(A[mid] < A[mid + 1]\) the peak is to the right, else at or to the left. This takes \(O(\log n)\) comparisons. Then binary search the increasing part and the decreasing part, \(O(\log n)\) each. Total \(O(\log n)\).
A sorted array is a special bitonic array, and searching it needs \(\Omega(\log n)\) comparisons, so \(\Theta(\log n)\) is the best bound.

questions.text:
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the set of all functions from \(\{1, \ldots, n\}\) to \(\{0, 1\}\). Define the binary relation \(\preccurlyeq\) on \(\mathcal{F}\) as follows:

\(\forall f, g \in \mathcal{F},\ f \preccurlyeq g\) if and only if \(\forall x \in \{1, \ldots, n\},\ f(x) \leq g(x)\), where \(0 \leq 1\).

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
Each \(f\) is an \(n\)-bit vector, and \(\preccurlyeq\) is the componentwise order.
(A) False: the all-zero function \(\preccurlyeq\) the all-one function but not the reverse (for \(n \geq 1\)).
(B) True: reflexive (\(f(x) \leq f(x)\)), antisymmetric (\(f \preccurlyeq g\) and \(g \preccurlyeq f\) give \(f(x) = g(x)\) for all \(x\)), transitive (inequalities chain pointwise).
(C) True: any \(f, g\) have least upper bound \(\max(f(x), g(x))\) (pointwise OR) and greatest lower bound \(\min(f(x), g(x))\) (pointwise AND) in \(\mathcal{F}\). It is the Boolean lattice of subsets of \(\{1, \ldots, n\}\).
(D) False: it is not symmetric, so not an equivalence relation.

questions.text:
Given the following Karnaugh Map for a Boolean function \(F(w, x, y, z)\):

Which one or more of the following Boolean expression(s) represent(s) \(F\)?
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
With rows \(wx\) and columns \(yz\) in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10, the 1s are the four corners and the central 2 by 2 block. The corners are the cells with \(x = 0, z = 0\), giving \(\overline{x}\,\overline{z}\); the centre block is \(x = 1, z = 1\), giving \(xz\). So \(F = \overline{x}\,\overline{z} + xz\).
(A) The four minterms are exactly the four corners (\(\overline{x}\,\overline{z}\) with every \(w, y\)), plus \(xz\): equals F.
(B) Contains \(w\overline{x}yz\) (row 10, column 11), a 0 cell, and misses \(w\overline{x}\,\overline{y}\,\overline{z}\): wrong.
(C) Contains \(w\overline{x}\,\overline{y}z\) (row 10, column 01), a 0 cell, and misses \(\overline{x}y\overline{z}\) cells: wrong.
(D) Is the minimal form of F: correct.

questions.text:
Consider a system of linear equations \(PX = Q\) where \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}\) and \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}\). Suppose \(P\) has an LU decomposition, \(P = LU\), where

\[L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ l_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ l_{31} & l_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad U = \begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ 0 & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & u_{33} \end{bmatrix}.\]

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: The system \(PX = Q\) can be solved by first solving \(LY = Q\) and then \(UX = Y\).

options.label: B
options.text: If \(P\) is invertible, then both \(L\) and \(U\) are invertible.

options.label: C
options.text: If \(P\) is singular, then at least one of the diagonal elements of \(U\) is zero.

options.label: D
options.text: If \(P\) is symmetric, then both \(L\) and \(U\) are symmetric.

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
(A) True: \(LUX = Q\); put \(Y = UX\), solve \(LY = Q\) by forward substitution, then \(UX = Y\) by back substitution.
(B) True: \(\det P = \det L \det U = 1 \cdot u_{11}u_{22}u_{33}\). If \(\det P \neq 0\) then \(\det U \neq 0\), and \(\det L = 1\) always, so both are invertible.
(C) True: \(\det P = u_{11}u_{22}u_{33} = 0\) forces some \(u_{ii} = 0\).
(D) False: a triangular matrix is symmetric only if it is diagonal. For example \(P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) (extended to 3 by 3 with a 1) has \(L\) with \(l_{21} = 2\), which is not symmetric.

questions.text:
Consider a stack data structure into which we can PUSH and POP records. Assume that each record pushed in the stack has a positive integer key and that all keys are distinct.

We wish to augment the stack data structure with an \(O(1)\) time MIN operation that returns a pointer to the record with smallest key present in the stack

1) without deleting the corresponding record, and

2) without increasing the complexities of the standard stack operations.

Which one or more of the following approach(es) can achieve it?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep with every record in the stack, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep a pointer to the record with the smallest key in the stack.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep an auxiliary array in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained in sorted order.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep a Min-Heap in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained.

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Arrays, Stacks, Queues and Linked Lists
questions.solution:
(A) Works. On PUSH, the new record stores a pointer to the smaller of the top record and the top's stored minimum: \(O(1)\). MIN compares the top record with the record its pointer names: \(O(1)\). POP just removes the top, and the records below still carry correct pointers.
(B) Fails. After popping the minimum record, finding the new minimum needs a scan of the stack, \(O(n)\).
(C) Fails. Inserting a key into a sorted array on PUSH (and deleting on POP) costs \(O(n)\), which makes PUSH and POP slower.
(D) Fails. Heap insertion costs \(O(\log n)\) on PUSH, and POP must delete an arbitrary key from the heap, so the stack operations become slower than \(O(1)\).

questions.text:
Consider the following relational schema along with all the functional dependencies that hold on them.

R1(A, B, C, D, E): \(\{D \rightarrow E,\ EA \rightarrow B,\ EB \rightarrow C\}\)

R2(A, B, C, D): \(\{A \rightarrow D,\ A \rightarrow B,\ C \rightarrow A\}\)

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
R1: A and D appear on no right side, so every key contains them. \(\{A, D\}^{+} = \{A, D, E, B, C\}\), so AD is the only key and the prime attributes are A and D. In \(D \rightarrow E\), D is not a superkey and E is not prime, so R1 violates 3NF.
R2: C appears on no right side. \(\{C\}^{+} = \{C, A, D, B\}\), so C is the only key and C is the only prime attribute. In \(A \rightarrow D\), A is not a superkey and D is not prime, so R2 violates 3NF.
Hence (C) and (D) are true, (A) and (B) are false.

questions.text:
Consider a demand paging system with three frames, and the following page reference string: 1 2 3 4 5 4 1 6 4 5 1 3 2. The contents of the frames are as follows initially and after each reference (from left to right):

| initially | after | | | | | | | | | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| - | 1* | 2* | 3* | 4* | 5* | 4 | 1 | 6* | 4 | 5 | 1* | 3* | 2* |
| - | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 | 2 |
| - | - | 2 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| - | - | - | 3 | 3 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 3 | 3 |

The *-marked references cause page replacements.

Which one or more of the following could be the page replacement policy/policies in use?

options.label: A
options.text: Least Recently Used page replacement policy

options.label: B
options.text: Least Frequently Used page replacement policy

options.label: C
options.text: Most Frequently Used page replacement policy

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
Read the victims off the table: on 4 page 2 goes, on 5 page 3, on 6 page 1, on the second 1 page 4, on 3 page 5, and on 2 page 6.

(A) LRU: on 4 the frames hold 1, 2, 3 and page 1 is the least recently used, but 2 was replaced. Not LRU.

(B) LFU, counting every reference so far: on 6 the frames hold 1 (2 references), 4 (2) and 5 (1), so LFU evicts 5, but 1 was replaced. Not LFU.

(C) MFU, counting every reference so far: on 3 the frames hold 6 (1 reference), 1 (3 references: the 1st, 7th and 11th) and 5 (2), so MFU evicts 1, but 5 was replaced. Not MFU.

(D) Optimal evicts the page used furthest in the future. On 4: next uses are 1 at reference 7, 3 at 12, 2 at 13, so evict 2. On 5: 4 at 6, 1 at 7, 3 at 12, so evict 3. On 6: 4 at 9, 5 at 10, 1 at 11, so evict 1. From the second 1 on, none of the pages in memory is used again before the string ends, so any victim is optimal, including those in the table.

So only D.

questions.text:
\(P = \{P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\}\) consists of all active processes in an operating system.

\(R = \{R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4\}\) consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the system.

The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges.

Assignment edges: \(R_1 \rightarrow P_1\), \(R_2 \rightarrow P_2\), \(R_3 \rightarrow P_3\), \(R_4 \rightarrow P_4\) (the assignment edge \(R_1 \rightarrow P_1\) means resource \(R_1\) is assigned to process \(P_1\), and so on for others)

Claim edges: \(P_1 \rightarrow R_2\), \(P_2 \rightarrow R_3\), \(P_3 \rightarrow R_1\), \(P_2 \rightarrow R_4\), \(P_4 \rightarrow R_2\) (the claim edge \(P_1 \rightarrow R_2\) means process \(P_1\) is waiting for resource \(R_2\), and so on for others)

Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: Aborting \(P_1\) makes the system deadlock free.

options.label: B
options.text: Aborting \(P_3\) makes the system deadlock free.

options.label: C
options.text: Aborting \(P_2\) makes the system deadlock free.

options.label: D
options.text: Aborting \(P_1\) and \(P_4\) makes the system deadlock free.

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
With single-instance resources, a cycle means deadlock. Wait-for relations: \(P_1\) waits for \(P_2\) (R2), \(P_2\) waits for \(P_3\) (R3) and \(P_4\) (R4), \(P_3\) waits for \(P_1\) (R1), \(P_4\) waits for \(P_2\) (R2). Cycles: \(P_1 \rightarrow P_2 \rightarrow P_3 \rightarrow P_1\) and \(P_2 \rightarrow P_4 \rightarrow P_2\).
(A) Aborting \(P_1\) breaks the first cycle, but \(P_2\) and \(P_4\) still wait for each other: deadlock remains.
(B) Aborting \(P_3\) likewise leaves the \(P_2\), \(P_4\) cycle: deadlock remains.
(C) Aborting \(P_2\) breaks both cycles (it is in both). R2 goes to \(P_1\) or \(P_4\); each can finish in turn, then \(P_3\) gets R1. Deadlock free.
(D) Aborting \(P_1\) and \(P_4\) frees R1 and R4. \(P_3\) gets R1, finishes and frees R3; \(P_2\) then gets R3 and R4 and finishes. Deadlock free.

questions.text:
Three floating point numbers \(X, Y\), and \(Z\) are stored in three registers \(\text{R}_\text{X}\), \(\text{R}_\text{Y}\), and \(\text{R}_\text{Z}\), respectively in IEEE 754 single precision format as given below in hexadecimal:

\(\text{R}_\text{X}\) = 0xC1100000, \(\text{R}_\text{Y}\) = 0x40C00000, and \(\text{R}_\text{Z}\) = 0x41400000

Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
questions.subject: Digital Logic

questions.text: Which of the following Boolean algebraic equation(s) is/are CORRECT?
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
(A) Wrong. The left side is the minterms (with ABC as bits) 3, 4, 0, 5, 7, that is \(\{0, 3, 4, 5, 7\}\). The right side: \(BC = \{3, 7\}\), \(\overline{B}\,\overline{C} = \{0, 4\}\), \(\overline{A}\,\overline{B} = \{0, 1\}\), giving \(\{0, 1, 3, 4, 7\}\). They differ at 1 and 5.
(B) Correct: consensus theorem, \(BC = BC(A + \overline{A}) = ABC + \overline{A}BC\), absorbed by \(AB\) and \(\overline{A}C\).
(C) Correct: \((A + C)(\overline{A} + B) = A\overline{A} + AB + \overline{A}C + BC = AB + \overline{A}C + BC = AB + \overline{A}C\) by consensus.
(D) Correct: by De Morgan the complement of the product is the sum of the complements: \(\overline{A}BD + \overline{C}\,\overline{D} + A\overline{C}\,\overline{D} + \overline{A}\,\overline{B}D = \overline{A}D(B + \overline{B}) + \overline{C}\,\overline{D}(1 + A) = \overline{A}D + \overline{C}\,\overline{D}\).

questions.text:
Consider two grammars \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) with the production rules given below:

\(G_1\): \(S \rightarrow \textit{if } E \textit{ then } S \mid \textit{if } E \textit{ then } S \textit{ else } S \mid a\)
\(\quad E \rightarrow b\)

\(G_2\): \(S \rightarrow \textit{if } E \textit{ then } S \mid M\)
\(\quad M \rightarrow \textit{if } E \textit{ then } M \textit{ else } S \mid c\)
\(\quad E \rightarrow b\)

where \(\textit{if}, \textit{then}, \textit{else}, a, b, c\) are the terminals.

Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
G1 is the dangling-else grammar. Its first two S-productions both start with \(\textit{if}\), so it is not LL(1), and it is ambiguous: \(\textit{if } b \textit{ then if } b \textit{ then } a \textit{ else } a\) has two parse trees.

G2 is not LL(1) either: \(\text{FIRST}(\textit{if } E \textit{ then } S) = \{\textit{if}\}\) and \(\text{FIRST}(M) = \{\textit{if}, c\}\) overlap, so on \(\textit{if}\) the parser cannot choose an S-production.

G2 is also ambiguous. The S after an else can be an unmatched if, so an M can end in one. Take \(\textit{if } b \textit{ then if } b \textit{ then } c \textit{ else if } b \textit{ then } c \textit{ else } c\).

Tree 1: \(S \Rightarrow M \Rightarrow \textit{if } E \textit{ then } M_1 \textit{ else } c\), with \(M_1 = \textit{if } b \textit{ then } c \textit{ else } S\) and that \(S = \textit{if } b \textit{ then } c\).

Tree 2: \(S \Rightarrow \textit{if } E \textit{ then } S_1\), with \(S_1 \Rightarrow M = \textit{if } b \textit{ then } c \textit{ else } S_2\) and \(S_2 \Rightarrow M = \textit{if } b \textit{ then } c \textit{ else } c\).

So neither grammar is LL(1) and both are ambiguous: C and D.

questions.text:
Let \(\Sigma = \{a, b, c\}\). For \(x \in \Sigma^{*}\), and \(\alpha \in \Sigma\), let \(\#_{\alpha}(x)\) denote the number of occurrences of \(\alpha\) in \(x\).

Which one or more of the following option(s) define(s) regular language(s)?
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
(A) \(a^{*}b^{*}\): regular.
(B) Strings with no c force \(m - n = 0\), so the set is \(\{a^{n}b^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}\): not regular.
(C) Counting a's modulo 7 and b's modulo 9 needs a product DFA of \(7 \times 9 = 63\) states: regular.
(D) Intersect with \(a^{*}b^{*}\) to get \(\{a^{n}b^{n} \mid n \equiv 2 \pmod 7\}\), which is not regular (pumping lemma), and regular languages are closed under intersection, so (D) is not regular.

questions.text:
Consider the database transactions T1 and T2, and data items X and Y. Which of the schedule(s) is/are conflict serializable?

| Transaction T1 | Transaction T2 |
|---|---|
| R1(X) | W2(X) |
| W1(Y) | W2(Y) |
| R1(X) | COMMIT(T2) |
| W1(X) | |
| COMMIT(T1) | |

options.label: A
options.text: R1(X), W2(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(X), COMMIT(T2), COMMIT(T1)

options.label: B
options.text: W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)

options.label: C
options.text: R1(X), W1(Y), W2(X), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(X), COMMIT(T1), COMMIT(T2)

options.label: D
options.text: W2(X), R1(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)

questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
Draw the precedence graph from conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write).
(A) R1(X) before W2(X) gives T1 to T2; W2(X) before the second R1(X) gives T2 to T1. Cycle: not conflict serializable.
(B) W2(X) before R1(X), R1(X), W1(X) gives T2 to T1; W2(Y) before W1(Y) gives T2 to T1. No cycle: conflict serializable, equivalent to T2 then T1.
(C) R1(X) before W2(X) gives T1 to T2; W2(X) before the second R1(X) gives T2 to T1. Cycle: not conflict serializable.
(D) W2(X) before R1(X) gives T2 to T1; W1(Y) before W2(Y) gives T1 to T2. Cycle: not conflict serializable.

questions.text:
Consider the following relational schema:

Students (rollno: integer, name: string, age: integer, cgpa: real)

Courses (courseno: integer, cname: string, credits: integer)

Enrolled (rollno: integer, courseno: integer, grade: string)

Which of the following options is/are correct SQL query/queries to retrieve the names of the students enrolled in course number (i.e., courseno) 1470?

options.label: A
options.text:
SELECT S.name
FROM Students S
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Enrolled E
              WHERE E.courseno = 1470
                      AND E.rollno = S.rollno);

options.label: B
options.text:
SELECT S.name
FROM Students S
WHERE SIZEOF (SELECT * FROM Enrolled E
              WHERE E.courseno = 1470
                      AND E.rollno = S.rollno) > 0;

options.label: C
options.text:
SELECT S.name
FROM Students S
WHERE  0 < (SELECT COUNT(*)
            FROM Enrolled E
            WHERE E.courseno = 1470
                      AND E.rollno = S.rollno);

options.label: D

questions.subject: Databases
questions.chapter: Relational Algebra, Tuple Calculus and SQL
questions.solution:
(A) Correct. The correlated EXISTS subquery is true exactly when the student has an Enrolled row for course 1470.
(B) Wrong. SIZEOF is not an SQL function; the query is not valid SQL.
(C) Correct. The correlated COUNT(*) is positive exactly when the student is enrolled in 1470.
(D) Correct. Students and Enrolled share only the attribute rollno, so NATURAL JOIN joins on rollno, and the WHERE clause keeps the rows for course 1470.

questions.text:
Given a computing system with two levels of cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. The first level (L1) cache access time is 1 nanosecond (ns) and the “hit rate” for L1 cache is 90% while the processor is accessing the data from L1 cache. Whereas, for the second level (L2) cache, the “hit rate” is 80% and the “miss penalty” for transferring data from L2 cache to L1 cache is 10 ns. The “miss penalty” for the data to be transferred from main memory to L2 cache is 100 ns.

Then the average memory access time in this system in nanoseconds is ___________ . (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture

questions.text: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 180, 250, 150, 170, and 250, respectively, in nanoseconds. The delay of an inter-stage latch is 10 nanoseconds. Assume that there are no pipeline stalls due to branches and other hazards. The time taken to process 1000 instructions in microseconds is __________ . (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
Clock cycle \(=\) largest stage delay \(+\) latch delay \(= 250 + 10 = 260\) ns.
For \(n\) instructions on a \(k\)-stage pipeline: \((k + n - 1)\) cycles \(= 5 + 999 = 1004\) cycles.
Time \(= 1004 \times 260 = 261040\) ns \(= 261.04\) \(\mu\)s.

questions.text:
In a B+- tree where each node can hold at most four key values, a root to leaf path consists of the following nodes:

A = (49, 77, 83, -), B = (7, 19, 33, 44), C = (20*, 22*, 25*, 26*)

The *-marked keys signify that these are data entries in a leaf.

Assume that a pointer between keys \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) points to a subtree containing keys in \([k_1, k_2)\), and that when a leaf is created, the smallest key in it is copied up into its parent.

A record with key value 23 is inserted into the B+- tree.

The smallest key value in the parent of the leaf that contains 25* is __________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
Leaf C is full, so inserting 23 splits it: the five entries 20, 22, 23, 25, 26 become (20, 22) and (23, 25, 26), and 23, the smallest key of the new leaf, is copied up into B.
B would become (7, 19, 23, 33, 44), more than four keys, so B splits: the middle key 23 moves up into A, B keeps (7, 19) and a new node B' gets (33, 44).
The leaf (23, 25, 26) holds keys in [23, 33), so it hangs from the leftmost pointer of B' = (33, 44). The smallest key in that parent is 33.
(Splitting the leaf as (20, 22, 23) and (25, 26) copies up 25 instead; B's split then pushes 25 up and the leaf (25, 26) again hangs from (33, 44), so the answer is 33 either way.)

questions.text:
A computer system supports a logical address space of \(2^{32}\) bytes. It uses two-level hierarchical paging with a page size of 4096 bytes. A logical address is divided into a \(b\)-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.

The value of \(b\) is ___________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
Page offset: \(4096 = 2^{12}\), so 12 bits.
One page of the inner page table holds \(\frac{4096}{8} = 512 = 2^{9}\) entries, so the index within an inner page table page is 9 bits.
\(b = 32 - 12 - 9 = 11\).

questions.text:
Consider the following algorithm someAlgo that takes an undirected graph \(G\) as input.

```text
someAlgo(G)

   1. Let v be any vertex in G. Run BFS on G starting at
      v. Let u be a vertex in G at maximum distance from
      v as given by the BFS.
   2. Run BFS on G again with u as the starting vertex.
      Let z be the vertex at maximum distance from u as
      given by the BFS.
   3. Output the distance between u and z in G.
```

The output of someAlgo(\(T\)) for the tree shown in the given figure is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution:
On a tree, the double BFS finds the diameter: the first BFS ends at an endpoint u of a longest path, and the second BFS from u reaches the other end z. So the output is the number of edges on the longest path in the tree.
In the figure, the vertex of degree 4 near the centre (call it h) joins two leaves, the vertex e on the left and the vertex l on the right. From e hang a leaf, a path of two edges down to the lower left leaf, and the vertex c, which has two leaves. From l hang a leaf and a path of two edges to the rightmost leaf.
The longest path runs from the lower left leaf through its parent, e, h, l and the next vertex to the rightmost leaf: 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6 edges (the path from a leaf of c to the rightmost leaf is also 6). No path is longer, so the output is 6.

questions.text:
Let \(\Sigma = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\). For \(x \in \Sigma^{*}\), let \(prod(x)\) be the product of symbols in \(x\) modulo 7. We take \(prod(\epsilon) = 1\), where \(\epsilon\) is the null string.

For example, \(prod(124) = (1 \times 2 \times 4) \bmod 7 = 1\).

Define \(L = \{x \in \Sigma^{*} \mid prod(x) = 2\}\).

The number of states in a minimum state DFA for \(L\) is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
Track the product modulo 7. Every symbol is 1 to 4, none divisible by 7, so the product is never 0: the possible states are the residues 1 to 6.
All six are reachable from 1: 1, 2 (via 2), 3 (via 3), 4 (via 4), \(2 \times 3 = 6\), \(3 \times 4 = 12 \equiv 5\).
They are pairwise distinguishable: the nonzero residues form a group, so from state \(r\) the string with product \(2r^{-1}\) is accepted, and from any other state \(s \neq r\) the same string gives \(s \cdot 2r^{-1} \neq 2\). No dead state is needed since every residue can still reach 2.
So the minimum DFA has 6 states.

arr = {30, 50, 10, 0, 0}. ptr = &arr[0] + 1 points to arr[1].
a = *ptr = 50.
(*ptr)++ makes arr[1] = 51.
ptr++ moves ptr to arr[2], so *ptr = 10.
Printed value: a + *ptr + arr[1] = 50 + 10 + 51 = 111.

questions.text:
A quadratic polynomial \((x - \alpha)(x - \beta)\) over complex numbers is said to be square invariant if \((x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = (x - \alpha^{2})(x - \beta^{2})\). Suppose from the set of all square invariant quadratic polynomials we choose one at random.

The probability that the roots of the chosen polynomial are equal is __________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
The polynomials are equal exactly when the root multisets match: \(\{\alpha, \beta\} = \{\alpha^{2}, \beta^{2}\}\).
Case 1: \(\alpha = \alpha^{2}\) and \(\beta = \beta^{2}\). Then \(\alpha, \beta \in \{0, 1\}\), giving \(x^{2}\), \(x(x - 1)\), \((x - 1)^{2}\).
Case 2: \(\alpha = \beta^{2}\) and \(\beta = \alpha^{2}\). Then \(\alpha = \alpha^{4}\), so \(\alpha = 0\) or \(\alpha^{3} = 1\). \(\alpha = 0\) or 1 repeats case 1. \(\alpha = \omega\) (a primitive cube root of unity) gives \(\beta = \omega^{2}\), the polynomial \((x - \omega)(x - \omega^{2}) = x^{2} + x + 1\).
So there are 4 square invariant polynomials: \(x^{2}\), \(x^{2} - x\), \(x^{2} - 2x + 1\), \(x^{2} + x + 1\). Two of them (\(x^{2}\) and \((x - 1)^{2}\)) have equal roots.
Probability \(= \frac{2}{4} = 0.5\).
